title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 50
paragraphs: Croesus sent all of this to Delphi, along with much more: two enormous mixing bowls, one gold and one silver. The gold one was placed to the right as you enter the temple, the silver one to the left. Both were moved after the temple fire. The gold bowl now sits in the treasury of the people of Clazomenai, weighing eight and a half talents plus twelve extra pounds. The silver one stands in the corner of the vestibule and holds six hundred amphors—the Delphians fill it with wine for the festival of the Theophania. The Delphians say it is the work of Theodoros the Samian, and I believe them. The craftsmanship is clearly exceptional. Croesus also sent four silver wine jars, now in the Corinthian treasury, and two vessels for holy water—one gold, one silver. The gold one bears the inscription "from the Spartans," who claim it as their offering. But they are wrong. This too came from Croesus. A man of Delphi wrote the inscription to please the Spartans. I know his name but will not mention it. The bronze boy through whose hands the water flows is indeed a Spartan gift, but neither of the water vessels came from them. Along with these, Croesus sent many other offerings not specially distinguished, including round silver castings and a golden statue of a woman three cubits tall, which the Delphians say represents Croesus' baker. He also dedicated the jewelry from his wife's neck and her girdles.
